quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A drought is not simply a period without rain; it is a shortage of water relative to what is normal for a region. A desert may go months without rain and still not be in drought, because its plants and animals are adapted to dryness. In a rainy region, however, three weeks without rain can cause serious problems for farmers. Governments therefore compare current rainfall with long-term averages for the same area. Droughts can develop slowly and are often noticed only after crops begin to fail. Early warning systems track soil moisture as well as rainfall. Farmers in affected areas may be offered financial help once officials declare a drought.
quests.question: A desert that has had no rain for months is not automatically in drought.
quests.hint: Recall that drought is measured against what is normal.
quests.explanation: A desert's living things are adapted to dryness, so months without rain need not be a drought.
quests.evidenceLine: A desert may go months without rain and still not be in drought, because its plants and animals are adapted to dryness.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Jet lag is usually worse when traveling east than when traveling west. Flying east means the body clock must be advanced, so people have to fall asleep earlier than they feel ready to. Flying west lengthens the day, which is easier to adjust to. Some travelers try to prepare by shifting their sleep times a few days before departure. Sunlight at the right times of day also helps the body clock adapt. Melatonin supplements have been used, although their effects vary. Airline crews, who cross time zones constantly, often follow strict routines to reduce the problem.
quests.question: Traveling west generally causes worse jet lag than traveling east.
quests.hint: Which direction does the first sentence call worse?
quests.explanation: Traveling east is usually worse, so the statement is reversed.
quests.evidenceLine: Jet lag is usually worse when traveling east than when traveling west.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Cities in dry regions increasingly reuse water that has already been used in homes. After treatment, this recycled water is used to irrigate parks, flush toilets, and cool industrial plants. In a few places, it is treated further and added to drinking water supplies. Many residents initially reacted with disgust, even though the water meets strict safety standards. Public campaigns emphasize that all water on Earth has been used many times before. Acceptance grows when people can visit the treatment plants. Several cities now show the treatment process to schoolchildren during organized visits every spring.
quests.question: Reused water goes through treatment before it irrigates parks.
quests.hint: Look at what happens before the water is used.
quests.explanation: After treatment, the recycled water is used to irrigate parks.
quests.evidenceLine: After treatment, this recycled water is used to irrigate parks, flush toilets, and cool industrial plants.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: The Rosetta Stone, discovered in Egypt in 1799, carries the same text in three scripts: ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, a later Egyptian script, and Greek. Scholars could read Greek, so they had a key to the other two. The breakthrough came more than twenty years later, when a French scholar recognized that hieroglyphs could represent sounds as well as ideas. This allowed the reading of thousands of texts that had been silent for centuries. The stone is now displayed in a museum in London. It remains one of the museum's most visited objects. Museum guides say that visitors often queue for a long time to see it at busy periods.
quests.question: Being able to read Greek helped scholars decipher the other scripts.
quests.hint: What advantage did scholars have with the Greek?
quests.explanation: They could read Greek, so it served as a key to the other two scripts.
quests.evidenceLine: Scholars could read Greek, so they had a key to the other two.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: When a factory worker in a survey was asked what mattered most about a job, she did not mention salary first. She said that having a manager who listened was more important than a small pay increase. Studies of workplaces show similar results: employees who feel heard are less likely to leave. Replacing a worker can cost a company up to twice that person's annual salary. Some firms have therefore trained supervisors in listening skills. The results include lower turnover and fewer complaints. The company also began asking employees for anonymous feedback about their supervisors every quarter.
quests.question: Supervisors who listen may save a company money by keeping staff.
quests.hint: Link the effect on leaving with the cost of replacing workers.
quests.explanation: Heard employees are less likely to leave, and replacing a worker is very costly.
quests.evidenceLine: Studies of workplaces show similar results: employees who feel heard are less likely to leave. Replacing a worker can cost a company up to twice that person's annual salary.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Some people think that microwaves cook food from the inside out. In fact, microwaves heat the outer layers, typically to a depth of a few centimeters, and the heat then spreads inward. That is why the center of a thick dish may stay cold while the edges are hot. Stirring the food halfway through helps to spread the heat. Letting it stand for a minute before eating also allows the temperature to even out. Metal containers should not be used, since they can cause sparks. Instructions on frozen meals often repeat this advice by asking users to stir and wait.
quests.question: Microwaves warm the center of food before the outside.
quests.hint: Where does the heating begin?
quests.explanation: The outer layers heat first and the warmth spreads inward.
quests.evidenceLine: In fact, microwaves heat the outer layers, typically to a depth of a few centimeters, and the heat then spreads inward.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Farmers sometimes plant beans between rows of corn. The corn plants provide a support for the beans to climb, and the beans, in turn, add nitrogen to the soil. Nitrogen is a nutrient that corn needs in large amounts. This combination has been used by Native American farmers for centuries. Together with squash, which shades the ground and reduces weeds, it is known as the "three sisters." The system needs less fertilizer than growing corn alone. Modern organic farmers are rediscovering the method because it reduces the need to buy chemical products.
quests.question: Beans take nitrogen from the soil and leave less for the corn.
quests.hint: What do the beans do for the soil?
quests.explanation: They add nitrogen, which corn needs, rather than removing it.
quests.evidenceLine: The corn plants provide a support for the beans to climb, and the beans, in turn, add nitrogen to the soil.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: When Yara's grandmother moved into their house, everyone expected that the arrangement would be difficult. Her parents worried about noise and privacy, and Yara herself feared that she would lose her room. In the end, the grandmother took the small study downstairs, and Yara kept her room. Within a few weeks, the family found that mealtimes became livelier and that Yara's younger brother did his homework more willingly. Her mother admits that her fears were exaggerated. The grandmother, however, misses her old garden. Her father has since built a small greenhouse so that she can garden at home.
quests.question: Yara had to give up her room for her grandmother.
quests.hint: Where did the grandmother end up sleeping?
quests.explanation: She took the small study downstairs, and Yara kept her room.
quests.evidenceLine: In the end, the grandmother took the small study downstairs, and Yara kept her room.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A teacher in a village school noticed that children who arrived hungry struggled to concentrate. She asked local farmers to donate fruit, and the school began offering a small breakfast. Over the next year, the number of students who were late dropped, and reading scores improved. Not every improvement can be credited to the breakfast, since a new library also opened during that time. Even so, the teacher and parents are convinced that it played a large part. Other schools in the district have begun similar programs. The district plans to publish a report on the results next spring.
quests.question: The breakfast may not be the only reason for the improvement.
quests.hint: Look for the other event that happened at the same time.
quests.explanation: A new library also opened, so not every improvement can be credited to the breakfast.
quests.evidenceLine: Not every improvement can be credited to the breakfast, since a new library also opened during that time.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Documentary makers face an ethical question: how much should they interfere with the events they film? Some believe that the camera should simply observe, while others argue that a film-maker who sees someone in danger has a duty to act. A few directors have been criticized for staging scenes and presenting them as real. Audiences generally accept the use of music and editing, but they expect the story itself to be true. Awards committees have started to ask for details of how key scenes were made. The debate is unlikely to end soon. Some film schools now include a course that discusses these questions with working directors.
quests.question: Audiences tolerate editing and music but expect the events themselves to be true.
quests.hint: What do audiences accept, and what do they expect?
quests.explanation: They accept music and editing but expect the story to be true.
quests.evidenceLine: Audiences generally accept the use of music and editing, but they expect the story itself to be true.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Many people think that the Vikings wore horned helmets in battle. There is no archaeological evidence for this; the only well-preserved Viking helmet found so far is rounded and has no horns. The image seems to have been popularized by a nineteenth-century costume designer for an opera. Horns would also have been impractical in a fight, since they could catch an opponent's weapon. Vikings were nevertheless skilled sailors and traders as well as raiders. Museums now try to correct the popular picture. Popular children's books and cartoons continue to show the horns, and the image is hard to remove.
quests.question: Archaeologists have found several Viking helmets with horns.
quests.hint: What has actually been found?
quests.explanation: Only one well-preserved helmet, and it has no horns.
quests.evidenceLine: There is no archaeological evidence for this; the only well-preserved Viking helmet found so far is rounded and has no horns.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Tourists in some cities are warned about "friendship bracelet" scams, in which a stranger ties a bracelet on their wrist and then demands money. The trick works because it is difficult to refuse a gift without seeming rude. Local police recommend keeping hands in pockets and saying a firm "no" at the first approach. Most vendors are honest and do not force anyone to pay. Travelers should learn to tell them apart. Ignoring a person completely is usually enough. Tourist offices in several cities have put up small signs to warn visitors.
quests.question: Local police advise tourists to accept the bracelet politely and pay for it.
quests.hint: What do police recommend at the first approach?
quests.explanation: They recommend keeping hands in pockets and saying a firm no.
quests.evidenceLine: Local police recommend keeping hands in pockets and saying a firm "no" at the first approach.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Antarctica is the driest continent on Earth, despite being covered by ice. Very little snow falls, and the cold air holds almost no moisture. In the interior, the annual snowfall is less than that of many deserts. The ice sheet is thick because snow that fell over hundreds of thousands of years has been compressed. If it melted, global sea levels would rise by tens of meters. Scientists therefore monitor it closely. Research stations there are supplied by aircraft and ships during the short summer season.
quests.question: Antarctica's thick ice built up over a very long period.
quests.hint: Find the explanation for the thickness of the ice.
quests.explanation: The ice thickened as snow from hundreds of thousands of years was compressed.
quests.evidenceLine: The ice sheet is thick because snow that fell over hundreds of thousands of years has been compressed.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Sitting for long periods is linked to higher risks of heart disease and diabetes. Interestingly, studies suggest that a daily workout does not fully cancel the effects of many hours of sitting. Short breaks to stand or walk every half hour appear to help. Standing desks can also be useful, although standing for many hours brings its own problems. Experts therefore recommend alternating between sitting, standing, and walking. Even simple stretching at the desk can improve circulation. Some companies now provide desks that allow employees to change position easily.
quests.question: A daily workout fully cancels the harm of sitting for many hours.
quests.hint: What do studies say about a workout and long sitting?
quests.explanation: A workout does not fully cancel the effects, so completely removing them is wrong.
quests.evidenceLine: Interestingly, studies suggest that a daily workout does not fully cancel the effects of many hours of sitting.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Most drowning victims are not people who are splashing and calling for help. Real drowning is often quiet: a person's mouth is at water level, arms press downward, and there is no breath to shout. Lifeguards are therefore trained to look for a vertical body in the water and eyes that look glazed. Parents are advised to stay within arm's reach of small children near water. Inflatable toys and armbands should never replace supervision. A silent child in a pool deserves immediate attention. Swimming schools teach children to recognize the signs of trouble in other swimmers.
quests.question: Drowning is often silent rather than noisy.
quests.hint: Read how a real drowning looks and sounds.
quests.explanation: The passage says real drowning is often quiet.
quests.evidenceLine: Real drowning is often quiet: a person's mouth is at water level, arms press downward, and there is no breath to shout.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Children who grow up bilingual sometimes mix words from both languages in the same sentence. Parents worry that this is a sign of confusion, but linguists disagree. Mixing usually follows rules and shows that the child is aware of both grammars. Bilingual children may also begin to speak slightly later than others, but by school age they usually catch up. Studies suggest that managing two languages can improve certain kinds of attention. Experts advise parents to keep speaking their native language at home. Teachers can help by welcoming both languages in the classroom without correcting the mixing.
quests.question: Linguists agree that mixing languages shows a child is confused.
quests.hint: What do the linguists say about the parents' worry?
quests.explanation: Linguists disagree with the worry and see mixing as rule-governed.
quests.evidenceLine: Parents worry that this is a sign of confusion, but linguists disagree.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: When a currency loses value against others, imports become more expensive. A country that buys most of its fuel abroad will therefore see gasoline prices rise. On the other hand, its exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, which can help factories and farmers. Tourists from abroad also find the country a better bargain. Governments must balance these effects, since higher prices can hurt households. Central banks sometimes intervene to slow rapid changes. Travel agencies often advertise special offers for visitors when the local currency is weak.
quests.question: A falling currency makes a country's exports more expensive for foreign buyers.
quests.hint: What happens to exports when the currency weakens?
quests.explanation: Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, not more expensive.
quests.evidenceLine: On the other hand, its exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, which can help factories and farmers.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Whole grains include the bran, the germ, and the endosperm of the seed. In refined grains, such as white flour, the bran and germ are removed, which reduces fiber and some vitamins. Nutritionists therefore recommend choosing whole grains when possible. However, refined grains are not harmful in small amounts, and many people prefer their softer texture. Labels can be confusing, since "wheat bread" may be made mostly from refined flour. The ingredient list is the best guide. Some bakeries now label their loaves with the percentage of whole grain they contain.
quests.question: Anything labeled wheat bread is made from whole grains.
quests.hint: Read the sentence about confusing labels.
quests.explanation: "Wheat bread" may be made mostly from refined flour, so the label does not guarantee whole grains.
quests.evidenceLine: Labels can be confusing, since "wheat bread" may be made mostly from refined flour.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: In many cultures, food is central to hospitality, but the rules differ. In Japan, finishing all the rice in a bowl is considered polite, because it shows appreciation. In some other countries, leaving a little food on the plate signals that the host has been generous. In parts of the Middle East, a host who does not urge guests to take more may be seen as stingy. Travelers who are unsure are usually best advised to watch what their hosts do. Small mistakes are typically forgiven if the guest is polite. Guidebooks written for business travelers often warn about such differences before meetings and dinners.
quests.question: Leaving food on the plate is polite in some countries and impolite in others.
quests.hint: Compare the Japanese custom with the one in the other countries.
quests.explanation: Japan treats finishing the food as polite, while elsewhere leaving a little shows the host's generosity.
quests.evidenceLine: In Japan, finishing all the rice in a bowl is considered polite, because it shows appreciation. In some other countries, leaving a little food on the plate signals that the host has been generous.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Some people think that owls can turn their heads all the way around. In reality, an owl can rotate its head about 270 degrees, which is impressive but not a full circle. This flexibility compensates for the fact that owls cannot move their eyes; the eyes are fixed in their sockets. Special blood vessels in the neck prevent damage to the brain during rapid turns. Owls also have very good hearing, which helps them find prey in the dark. Their feathers are soft, so they fly almost silently. Zookeepers say that watching owls in the evening is the best way to notice these abilities.
quests.question: Owls can move their eyes freely in their sockets.
quests.hint: What does the passage say about owls' eye movement?
quests.explanation: The eyes are fixed in their sockets, so owls cannot move them.
quests.evidenceLine: This flexibility compensates for the fact that owls cannot move their eyes; the eyes are fixed in their sockets.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A common belief is that individual actions like recycling make no difference compared with the pollution caused by large industries. It is true that industry produces a large share of emissions. However, household choices affect demand, and demand shapes what companies produce. In addition, people who adopt one green habit often become more open to others. Politicians also pay attention when large numbers of voters change their behavior. Environmental groups therefore encourage both personal action and political pressure. Surveys suggest that people who recycle are more likely to support environmental laws too.
quests.question: Environmental groups say that personal action is pointless.
quests.hint: What do environmental groups encourage?
quests.explanation: They encourage both personal action and political pressure.
quests.evidenceLine: Environmental groups therefore encourage both personal action and political pressure.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Ayesha wanted to read more, but each evening she ended up watching videos instead. She realized that her phone was always within reach on the sofa, so she began charging it in another room. At first, she felt restless and picked up a book only out of boredom. After two weeks, she found herself looking forward to reading before bed. She now finishes about three books a month. She says the change required no willpower, only a different arrangement of her space. Her friends have started to leave their own phones in a basket during dinners.
quests.question: Ayesha found that rearranging her surroundings worked better than relying on willpower.
quests.hint: Read her own summary of the change.
quests.explanation: She says the change required no willpower, only a different arrangement of her space.
quests.evidenceLine: She says the change required no willpower, only a different arrangement of her space.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: In tropical regions, seasons are often defined by rainfall rather than temperature. A "wet season" may last from May to October, followed by a "dry season" with clear skies. Temperatures stay fairly constant throughout the year, varying by only a few degrees. Farmers plan their planting according to the arrival of the rains. If the rains come late, crops may fail. Forecasters therefore monitor ocean temperatures, which can signal delays. Some tropical countries also use satellites to measure the moisture of the soil.
quests.question: Tropical farmers time their planting by the arrival of the rains.
quests.hint: Which sentence describes how farmers plan?
quests.explanation: Farmers plan their planting according to the arrival of the rains.
quests.evidenceLine: Farmers plan their planting according to the arrival of the rains.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A city introduced free public transport on weekends in the hope of reducing car use. Ridership rose by forty percent, but a survey showed that most new passengers were previously walkers or cyclists. Only a small fraction had left their cars at home. Officials therefore concluded that the policy had increased travel without lowering traffic. The council is now considering ways to target drivers directly, such as cheaper monthly passes. The free weekend service will continue for now. Transport experts say that raising the price of city parking would probably work better.
quests.question: Most of the new passengers had previously been car drivers.
quests.hint: Who made up most of the new riders?
quests.explanation: Most were previously walkers or cyclists, and only a small fraction had left their cars.
quests.evidenceLine: Ridership rose by forty percent, but a survey showed that most new passengers were previously walkers or cyclists. Only a small fraction had left their cars at home.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: In cricket, a bowler who takes five wickets in a single innings is considered to have achieved something special. The feat is celebrated by having the player's name written on an honors board at some grounds. However, a bowler's success also depends on the batsmen's mistakes and on the condition of the pitch. Statisticians therefore look at averages over a whole career, not just individual matches. A bowler with a low average is usually more consistent. Consistency is prized by captains. Some statistics websites now list several different measures for every player.
quests.question: Statisticians prefer to judge bowlers by a single match.
quests.hint: How do statisticians prefer to judge bowlers?
quests.explanation: They look at averages over a whole career, not just individual matches.
quests.evidenceLine: Statisticians therefore look at averages over a whole career, not just individual matches.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Restaurants often set prices so that the second cheapest item looks attractive. A menu might list a small pizza at $9, a medium at $13, and a large at $14. Most customers choose the large, because the price difference between medium and large seems small. The restaurant earns the highest margin on the large size. This technique is called decoy pricing, since the medium pizza acts as a decoy. Customers who notice the effect can choose more thoughtfully. Restaurant managers say that changing one price on a menu can shift what people order.
quests.question: The medium pizza works as a decoy that pushes customers toward the large one.
quests.hint: What role does the medium size play?
quests.explanation: The passage calls it a decoy that makes the large size look like good value.
quests.evidenceLine: This technique is called decoy pricing, since the medium pizza acts as a decoy.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Landlords in some cities must provide a heating system that keeps rooms at a minimum temperature. Tenants who find their homes too cold should first tell the landlord in writing. If nothing is done within a reasonable time, they can contact the local housing office. The office may inspect the property and order repairs. Keeping a record of temperatures and dates strengthens a complaint. Tenants are advised not to withhold rent without legal advice. Many cities publish simple guides that explain these steps in several languages.
quests.question: Tenants should inform the landlord in writing before contacting the housing office.
quests.hint: Put the tenants' steps in order.
quests.explanation: They should first tell the landlord in writing, and only then contact the housing office.
quests.evidenceLine: Tenants who find their homes too cold should first tell the landlord in writing. If nothing is done within a reasonable time, they can contact the local housing office.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A study of software teams found that the best managers were not necessarily the most technically skilled. Instead, they listened well, gave clear feedback, and helped team members to solve problems on their own. Teams with such managers reported higher satisfaction and stayed together longer. Companies that promoted the best programmers to management often lost both a good programmer and a mediocre manager. Some firms now offer separate career paths for specialists and for managers. Employees can choose the one that suits them. The authors suggest that companies should offer training to managers before they take up the role.
quests.question: The study found that the most technically skilled programmers made the best managers.
quests.hint: What did the study conclude in its first sentence?
quests.explanation: The best managers were not necessarily the most technically skilled.
quests.evidenceLine: A study of software teams found that the best managers were not necessarily the most technically skilled.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Facial recognition systems compare an image of a face with a database of known faces. Accuracy has improved greatly, but studies have shown that error rates differ between groups of people. In some systems, women and people with darker skin were misidentified more often than others, because the training images included fewer of them. Some cities have restricted police use of the technology until these problems are solved. Developers say that more diverse training data can reduce the gap. Critics remain concerned about privacy. Independent testers now publish yearly reports that compare the performance of different systems.
quests.question: Unbalanced training images contributed to uneven error rates.
quests.hint: Find the cause given for the misidentifications.
quests.explanation: The training images included fewer women and people with darker skin.
quests.evidenceLine: In some systems, women and people with darker skin were misidentified more often than others, because the training images included fewer of them.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A museum decided to display paintings without labels for one month. Visitors had to look at each work and form their own impressions before reading about it. Many said that they spent more time in front of each painting than usual. Others complained that they missed the background information. The museum now offers labels on request, allowing visitors to choose. The experiment will be repeated with sculptures. The director said that visitors' comments would guide the design of future exhibitions.
quests.question: Some visitors were unhappy about lacking information on the paintings.
quests.hint: Look at the reactions of the "others."
quests.explanation: Others complained that they missed the background information.
quests.evidenceLine: Others complained that they missed the background information.
